subject: anatomy
prompt: An endoscope is used to examine the natural drainage opening of the maxillary sinus. In which nasal passage should this opening be sought?
explanation: The maxillary sinus opens high on its medial wall into the semilunar hiatus of the middle nasal meatus.

distractorExplanations.A: The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct, not the natural maxillary sinus opening.
distractorExplanations.C: The posterior ethmoidal cells open into the superior meatus.
distractorExplanations.D: This recess receives the sphenoidal sinus, not the maxillary sinus.

learningObjective: Locate the natural opening of the maxillary sinus.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Paranasal sinuses — maxillary sinus

subject: anatomy
prompt: A clinician follows the natural opening of the sphenoidal sinus into the nasal cavity. Where does the opening lead?

options.text: Nasopharyngeal opening of the auditory tube

explanation: The sphenoidal sinus opens onto the posterior roof of the nasal cavity in the spheno-ethmoidal recess.

distractorExplanations.A: The middle meatus receives frontal, maxillary, and anterior or middle ethmoidal drainage.
distractorExplanations.C: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus.
distractorExplanations.D: This opening connects the nasopharynx with the middle ear, not a paranasal sinus.

learningObjective: Distinguish sphenoidal sinus drainage from the drainage of other paranasal sinuses.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Paranasal sinuses — sphenoidal sinus

subject: anatomy
prompt: Excess tears enter the nose through the nasolacrimal duct. The duct opens beneath which nasal concha?

options.text: No concha; it opens directly into the nasopharynx

explanation: The duct opens into the inferior nasal meatus beneath the anterior lip of the inferior concha.

distractorExplanations.B: The middle meatus beneath this concha receives several paranasal sinus openings, not the nasolacrimal duct.
distractorExplanations.C: The superior meatus is associated with posterior ethmoidal drainage.
distractorExplanations.D: The duct opens on the lateral nasal wall, not directly into the nasopharynx.

learningObjective: Identify the nasal opening of the nasolacrimal duct.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Lateral wall — nasolacrimal duct

subject: anatomy
prompt: Infection is confined to the posterior ethmoidal air cells. Which nasal passage receives their usual drainage?

options.text: Semilunar hiatus in the middle meatus

explanation: Posterior ethmoidal cells usually open onto the lateral wall of the superior nasal meatus.

distractorExplanations.A: This meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct.
distractorExplanations.B: The semilunar hiatus is associated with maxillary and anterior sinus drainage, not the usual posterior ethmoidal openings.
distractorExplanations.C: The sphenoidal sinus opens here; posterior ethmoidal cells usually open into the superior meatus.

learningObjective: Differentiate anterior, middle, and posterior ethmoidal drainage.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Paranasal sinuses — ethmoidal cells

subject: anatomy
prompt: After a fracture involving the roof of the nasal cavity, a patient loses the sense of smell. Which structure normally transmits the injured olfactory axons into the cranial cavity?

options.text: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone

explanation: Bundles of olfactory receptor axons pass through small cribriform plate perforations to reach the olfactory bulb.

distractorExplanations.A: Foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve; it is not the route of olfactory axons.
distractorExplanations.B: The incisive canal connects the nasal floor and oral palate and carries the nasopalatine nerve and vessels.
distractorExplanations.D: This connects the pterygopalatine fossa and nasal cavity and transmits nasal neurovascular branches.

learningObjective: Relate olfactory nerve fibers to the cribriform plate.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Ethmoid bone; gateways — cribriform plate

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Walls, floor, and roof — nasal septum
prompt: A sagittal specimen shows the posterior bony part of the nasal septum. Which pair forms most of this part of the septum?

options.text: Vomer and perpendicular plate of the ethmoid
Palatine process of the maxilla and horizontal plate of the palatine

explanation: The posterior septum is formed mainly by the vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid; septal cartilage is anterior.

distractorExplanations.B: These contribute to the lateral nasal wall rather than most of the septum.
distractorExplanations.C: These form the hard palate and nasal floor, not the principal vertical posterior septum.
distractorExplanations.D: The nasal bone makes only a small septal contribution, and the zygomatic bone is not a principal septal component.

learningObjective: Identify the principal bones of the posterior nasal septum.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Walls, floor, and roof — nasal septum

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which of the following nasal conchae is a separate bone rather than a process of the ethmoid bone?
explanation: The inferior nasal concha is an independent paired bone. The superior and middle conchae belong to the ethmoid.

distractorExplanations.A: The middle concha is a process of the ethmoidal labyrinth.
distractorExplanations.C: The superior concha is also part of the ethmoid.
distractorExplanations.D: The uncinate process is an ethmoidal projection and is not a separate nasal concha.

learningObjective: Distinguish the inferior concha from the ethmoidal conchae.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Skeletal framework — nasal conchae

subject: anatomy
prompt: A patient has bleeding from the common superficial arterial anastomotic area of the nasal septum. Where is this area located?

options.text: Posterior roof over the sphenoidal sinus opening
Anterior region of the medial nasal wall
Lateral wall of the superior nasal meatus
Roof of the nasopharynx over the pharyngeal tonsil

explanation: Superficial anastomoses of greater palatine, sphenopalatine, superior labial, and anterior ethmoidal branches occur on the anterior septum.

distractorExplanations.A: The common superficial septal anastomotic area is anterior, not at the sphenoidal sinus opening.
distractorExplanations.C: This is not the anterior medial-wall anastomotic area described in the question.
distractorExplanations.D: The pharyngeal tonsil is posterior to the nasal cavity and does not identify this septal arterial area.

learningObjective: Locate the common septal site of epistaxis.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Vessels — arterial anastomoses and epistaxis

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which cranial nerve division supplies general sensation to the anterior region of the nasal cavity, chiefly through the anterior ethmoidal nerve?

options.text: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2)
Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1)

explanation: The anterior ethmoidal nerve is a nasociliary branch of V1; ophthalmic branches supply the anterior nasal region.

distractorExplanations.A: V2 supplies much of the posterior nasal cavity; it is not the parent division of the anterior ethmoidal nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: The olfactory nerve mediates smell, not general sensation.
distractorExplanations.D: Facial parasympathetic fibers provide secretomotor supply to nasal glands, not this general sensory pathway.

learningObjective: Separate nasal general sensation from olfaction and secretomotor innervation.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Innervation — trigeminal sensory supply

subject: anatomy
prompt: An infection around an upper molar root spreads into an adjacent paranasal sinus. Which sinus is most directly related to these roots?
explanation: The maxillary sinus is closely related inferiorly to the roots of upper molar and premolar teeth.

distractorExplanations.A: The frontal sinus is above the bridge of the nose and orbit, away from upper molar roots.
distractorExplanations.B: The sphenoidal sinus is within the sphenoid body and relates to the pituitary region, not directly to molar roots.
distractorExplanations.C: These lie in the ethmoidal labyrinth beside the nasal cavity and orbit, not adjacent to upper molar roots.

learningObjective: Apply the dental relationships of the maxillary sinus.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Paranasal sinuses — maxillary relations

subject: anatomy
prompt: At approximately which vertebral level does the pharynx become continuous with the esophagus in an adult?
explanation: The pharynx continues into the esophagus at approximately the level of C6.

distractorExplanations.A: C2 is well superior to the pharyngoesophageal junction.
distractorExplanations.C: This level is associated with the tracheal bifurcation, not the start of the esophagus.
distractorExplanations.D: T10 is associated with passage of the esophagus through the diaphragm, not its beginning.

learningObjective: Identify the inferior limit of the pharynx.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; General organization and inferior continuation

subject: anatomy
prompt: Enlarged adenoids obstruct a child’s nasal airway. Which site contains the lymphoid tissue responsible?

options.text: Between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches

explanation: The pharyngeal tonsil lies in the nasopharyngeal roof; when enlarged it is called the adenoids.

distractorExplanations.B: This site contains the palatine tonsil, not the pharyngeal tonsil.
distractorExplanations.C: This region contains the lingual tonsils.
distractorExplanations.D: The piriform fossa is a laryngopharyngeal channel beside the laryngeal inlet, not the location of the adenoids.

learningObjective: Locate the pharyngeal tonsil and relate enlargement to nasal obstruction.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nasopharynx — pharyngeal tonsil

subject: anatomy
prompt: The pharyngotympanic tube is followed medially from the middle ear. Into which region does it open?
explanation: The pharyngotympanic tube opens on the lateral nasopharyngeal wall, posterior and slightly superior to the hard palate.

distractorExplanations.A: The auditory tube opens above the soft palate in the nasopharynx.
distractorExplanations.B: The vestibule is inside the larynx and has no auditory tube opening.
distractorExplanations.C: The nasolacrimal duct, not the auditory tube, opens into the inferior nasal meatus.

learningObjective: Locate the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nasopharynx — pharyngotympanic tube

subject: anatomy
prompt: During examination of the open mouth, the palatine tonsil is seen between two mucosal arches. Which arches are these?
explanation: The palatine tonsil occupies the lateral oropharyngeal wall between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

distractorExplanations.A: These border the laryngeal inlet rather than the tonsillar fossa.
distractorExplanations.B: The vocal folds lie inside the larynx, well below the palatine tonsil.
distractorExplanations.D: The conchae project from the nasal lateral wall and do not border the palatine tonsil.

learningObjective: Identify the surface landmarks surrounding the palatine tonsil.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Oropharynx — palatine tonsil

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Longitudinal muscles; gaps in the pharyngeal wall
prompt: A dissection exposes a muscle entering the pharyngeal wall through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors. It is accompanied in this region by the glossopharyngeal nerve. Which muscle is it?
explanation: Stylopharyngeus descends from the styloid process and enters between the superior and middle constrictors; the glossopharyngeal nerve traverses this region.

distractorExplanations.A: Salpingopharyngeus descends from the auditory tube on the deep pharyngeal wall rather than entering by this gap.
distractorExplanations.B: Palatopharyngeus descends from the soft palate into the pharyngeal wall.
distractorExplanations.D: Cricothyroid is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle acting across the cricothyroid joint, not a longitudinal pharyngeal muscle.

learningObjective: Identify stylopharyngeus by its passage between the constrictors.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Longitudinal muscles; gaps in the pharyngeal wall

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which pharyngeal muscle is directly supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve rather than the vagus nerve?
explanation: Stylopharyngeus is supplied directly by IX. The other pharyngeal muscles receive motor supply from the vagus, mainly through the pharyngeal plexus.

distractorExplanations.A: The superior constrictor receives vagal motor innervation.
distractorExplanations.B: Palatopharyngeus receives vagal motor innervation.
distractorExplanations.C: Salpingopharyngeus is also supplied by the vagus nerve.

learningObjective: Recognize the motor exception among pharyngeal muscles.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — motor innervation

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Nasopharynx — closure of the pharyngeal isthmus
prompt: During swallowing, elevation of the soft palate combines with contraction of the palatopharyngeal sphincter. Which communication is thereby closed?

options.text: The choana between nasal cavity and nasopharynx
The rima glottidis between the vocal folds
The pharyngeal isthmus between nasopharynx and oropharynx

explanation: The elevated soft palate seals against the pharyngeal wall and closes the pharyngeal isthmus, separating the two regions.

distractorExplanations.A: The closure is inferior to the nasopharynx, not at the bony posterior nasal aperture.
distractorExplanations.B: Glottic closure involves intrinsic laryngeal mechanisms, not direct closure by the soft palate.
distractorExplanations.D: The bifurcation is in the thorax and is not closed by palatal movement.

learningObjective: Explain separation of the nasopharynx and oropharynx during swallowing.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nasopharynx — closure of the pharyngeal isthmus

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Nerves — sensory innervation and gag reflex
prompt: Touching the palatine tonsillar region normally initiates the afferent limb of the gag reflex. Which nerve carries this sensory input?
explanation: IX provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx and palatine tonsil and carries the afferent limb of the gag reflex.

distractorExplanations.A: XII supplies tongue muscles; it does not provide the tonsillar sensory limb of this reflex.
distractorExplanations.B: This vagal branch mainly supplies cricothyroid and part of the inferior constrictor, not tonsillar sensation.
distractorExplanations.C: V2 supplies nasopharyngeal sensation, whereas the oropharyngeal tonsillar region is supplied by IX.

learningObjective: Identify the sensory nerve of the oropharynx and afferent limb of the gag reflex.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — sensory innervation and gag reflex

subject: anatomy
prompt: During a deep inspiration, which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is chiefly responsible for abducting the vocal folds and widening the rima glottidis?
explanation: Posterior crico-arytenoid rotates the arytenoids laterally and abducts the vocal folds, opening the rima glottidis.

distractorExplanations.A: It rotates the arytenoids medially and adducts the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: It draws the arytenoid cartilages together rather than abducting them.
distractorExplanations.D: It lengthens and tensions the vocal folds rather than acting as their primary abductor.

learningObjective: Identify the primary abductor of the vocal folds.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic muscles — posterior crico-arytenoid

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Nerves — external laryngeal nerve and cricothyroid
prompt: After a neck operation, a singer has difficulty increasing vocal-fold tension. Injury to the nerve supplying cricothyroid is suspected. Which nerve is this?

options.text: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

explanation: The external laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid, whose action lengthens and tensions the vocal folds.

distractorExplanations.A: The internal branch is mainly sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: It supplies the other intrinsic laryngeal muscles, but not cricothyroid.
distractorExplanations.D: IX supplies stylopharyngeus and oropharyngeal sensation, not cricothyroid.

learningObjective: Associate cricothyroid with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — external laryngeal nerve and cricothyroid

subject: anatomy
prompt: A recurrent laryngeal nerve is injured. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle on that side retains its direct motor supply?
explanation: Cricothyroid is the intrinsic laryngeal exception: its motor supply is the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

distractorExplanations.A: Its direct motor supply is from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: This muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.C: Vocalis receives recurrent laryngeal motor fibers and therefore is not the spared exception.

learningObjective: Recognize the intrinsic laryngeal muscle spared by a recurrent laryngeal nerve lesion.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — recurrent laryngeal motor distribution

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Thyrohyoid membrane; nerves — internal laryngeal nerve
prompt: A sensory nerve reaches the larynx by piercing the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery. Which region is mainly supplied by this nerve?

options.text: Laryngeal mucosa below the vocal folds only
Laryngeal mucosa above the level of the vocal folds

explanation: The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and supplies the laryngeal cavity down to vocal-fold level.

distractorExplanations.A: Sensory supply below the folds comes from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the internal laryngeal cavity, not this cutaneous territory.
distractorExplanations.C: Anterior nasal general sensation is supplied by ophthalmic trigeminal branches, especially the anterior ethmoidal nerve.

learningObjective: Identify the sensory territory of the internal laryngeal nerve.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Thyrohyoid membrane; nerves — internal laryngeal nerve

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which nerve carries general sensation from the laryngeal cavity below the vocal folds?
explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is sensory below the vocal folds as well as motor to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

distractorExplanations.A: Its main sensory territory extends from above down to the level of the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: This branch supplies cricothyroid rather than the infraglottic sensory territory.
distractorExplanations.D: IX supplies oropharyngeal sensation, not the infraglottic cavity.

learningObjective: Identify sensory innervation of the infraglottic larynx.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Nerves — recurrent laryngeal sensory distribution

subject: anatomy
prompt: Contraction of cricothyroid pulls the thyroid cartilage forward and tilts it downward relative to the cricoid. What is the principal effect on the vocal ligaments?

options.text: They lengthen and become more tense
They shorten and become less tense
They are abducted primarily by lateral rotation of the arytenoids
They move superiorly to become vestibular ligaments

explanation: Forward and downward thyroid rotation increases the distance between the thyroid angle and arytenoid attachments, lengthening the vocal ligaments.

distractorExplanations.B: This is opposite to the effect of the described cricothyroid movement.
distractorExplanations.C: Primary abduction is produced by posterior crico-arytenoid acting at the crico-arytenoid joints.
distractorExplanations.D: Vocal and vestibular ligaments are distinct structures and do not transform into one another.

learningObjective: Relate cricothyroid joint movement to vocal-fold tension.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Laryngeal joints; cricothyroid action

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which unpaired intrinsic muscle spans between the posterior surfaces of the two arytenoid cartilages and draws them together?
explanation: The single transverse arytenoid spans between the arytenoids and adducts the cartilages.

distractorExplanations.B: This paired muscle runs from cricoid to arytenoid and abducts the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.C: Cricothyroid runs between cricoid and thyroid cartilages and tensions the vocal folds.
distractorExplanations.D: Vocalis runs alongside each vocal ligament and adjusts its tension; it does not span between the two arytenoids.

learningObjective: Identify the transverse arytenoid and its action.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic muscles — transverse arytenoid

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which intrinsic muscle rotates the arytenoid cartilage medially to adduct a vocal fold?
explanation: Lateral crico-arytenoid pulls on the muscular process to internally rotate the arytenoid and adduct the vocal fold.

distractorExplanations.A: It produces lateral rotation and abduction, the opposite movement.
distractorExplanations.C: It mainly lengthens the vocal fold through the cricothyroid joint.
distractorExplanations.D: This is a longitudinal pharyngeal muscle, not an intrinsic muscle acting on the arytenoid.

learningObjective: Link lateral crico-arytenoid action to closure of the vocal folds.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic muscles — lateral crico-arytenoid

subject: anatomy
prompt: The thickened free upper margin of the cricothyroid ligament forms which structure inside the larynx?
explanation: The free superior edge of the cricothyroid ligament is thickened into the vocal ligament beneath the true vocal fold.

distractorExplanations.A: The vestibular ligament is the thickened inferior edge of the quadrangular membrane.
distractorExplanations.B: This is an anterior midline thickening of the thyrohyoid membrane outside the laryngeal cavity.
distractorExplanations.C: This connects the lower cricoid border with the first tracheal cartilage.

learningObjective: Identify the ligament underlying the true vocal fold.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic ligaments — cricothyroid ligament

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which structure is formed by the thickened free lower margin of the quadrangular membrane?
explanation: The inferior free edge of the quadrangular membrane forms the vestibular ligament beneath the vestibular, or false vocal, fold.

distractorExplanations.A: The vocal ligament arises from the superior edge of the cricothyroid ligament below the quadrangular membrane.
distractorExplanations.B: This is the anterior midline thickening between thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
distractorExplanations.C: This attaches the epiglottis to the hyoid bone and is not an edge of the quadrangular membrane.

learningObjective: Identify the ligament underlying the false vocal fold.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic ligaments — quadrangular membrane

subject: anatomy
prompt: The posterior attachment of a vocal ligament is identified on an arytenoid cartilage. Which projection provides this attachment?

options.text: Inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage

explanation: The vocal ligament attaches posteriorly to the anteriorly projecting vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage.

distractorExplanations.A: The muscular process provides attachment for the posterior and lateral crico-arytenoid muscles.
distractorExplanations.B: The apex articulates with the corniculate cartilage, rather than anchoring the vocal ligament.
distractorExplanations.D: This horn articulates with the cricoid and is not the posterior attachment of the vocal ligament.

learningObjective: Distinguish the vocal and muscular processes of the arytenoid.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Laryngeal cartilages — arytenoid processes

subject: anatomy
prompt: In an anatomy teaching scenario, an emergency airway passes through the median cricothyroid ligament. Between which two cartilages is this ligament located?

options.text: Hyoid bone above and thyroid cartilage below
Cricoid cartilage above and first tracheal cartilage below
Thyroid cartilage above and cricoid cartilage below
Epiglottis anteriorly and arytenoid cartilage posteriorly

explanation: The median cricothyroid ligament spans the anterior interval between the inferior thyroid region and the arch of the cricoid.

distractorExplanations.A: This interval is crossed by the thyrohyoid membrane, not the median cricothyroid ligament.
distractorExplanations.B: This interval is crossed by the cricotracheal ligament.
distractorExplanations.D: The quadrangular membrane spans this region, not the median cricothyroid ligament.

learningObjective: Locate the median cricothyroid ligament relative to palpable laryngeal cartilages.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 8 — Head and Neck; Intrinsic ligaments — median cricothyroid ligament

subject: anatomy
prompt: The trachea begins near C6. At which vertebral level does it normally bifurcate into the main bronchi in the mediastinum?
explanation: Gray’s describes the trachea extending from C6 to its bifurcation at the T4/T5 level.

distractorExplanations.B: This is above the start of the trachea.
distractorExplanations.C: This is near the lower neck, not the normal mediastinal bifurcation.
distractorExplanations.D: This is much lower in the thorax than the tracheal bifurcation.

learningObjective: Locate the tracheal bifurcation.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchial tree — tracheal extent

subject: anatomy
prompt: On an axial section, the tracheal cartilages are C-shaped. Which description of the open part of each ring is correct?

options.text: It faces posteriorly, where the wall is mainly smooth muscle
It faces anteriorly and is completed by bone
It faces laterally and is completed by skeletal muscle
It faces superiorly and is closed by a vocal fold

explanation: The cartilaginous C is open posteriorly; the posterior tracheal wall is composed mainly of smooth muscle.

distractorExplanations.B: The open part faces posteriorly and is not completed by bone.
distractorExplanations.C: Neither the lateral orientation nor skeletal-muscle composition matches the tracheal wall.
distractorExplanations.D: The rings are transverse, and vocal folds belong to the larynx above the trachea.

learningObjective: Identify the posterior orientation and composition of the membranous tracheal wall.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchial tree — tracheal wall

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Bronchial tree — main bronchi and aspiration
prompt: A small inhaled foreign body enters a main bronchus. Which anatomical feature helps explain its greater tendency to enter the right side?

options.text: The left main bronchus is wider and more vertical
The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical
The right main bronchus has no cartilaginous support
The right main bronchus opens directly into the pleural cavity

explanation: The right main bronchus has a wider lumen and a more vertical course, favoring entry of inhaled material.

distractorExplanations.A: These features describe the right main bronchus, not the left.
distractorExplanations.C: Bronchi have cartilaginous support; absence of cartilage is characteristic of bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.D: It enters the lung through its root and hilum, not the pleural space.

learningObjective: Explain right-sided foreign-body entry using main-bronchus anatomy.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchial tree — main bronchi and aspiration

subject: anatomy
prompt: Bronchoscopy reveals a midline ridge separating the entrances to the right and left main bronchi. What is this ridge called?
explanation: The carina projects at the lower tracheal bifurcation between the origins of the two main bronchi.

distractorExplanations.A: The lingula is a tongue-like part of the left superior pulmonary lobe.
distractorExplanations.B: The hilum is the area on the medial lung surface where root structures enter and leave.
distractorExplanations.D: This is an inferior pleural fold extending from the lung root, not an intratracheal ridge.

learningObjective: Recognize the carina at the tracheal bifurcation.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchial tree — carina

subject: anatomy
prompt: How many lobar (secondary) bronchi normally supply the right and left lungs, respectively?

options.text: Two on the right and three on the left
Three on the right and two on the left

explanation: Each lobar bronchus supplies one lobe: the right lung has three lobes and the left has two.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the usual right and left lobe counts.
distractorExplanations.B: One main bronchus enters each lung, but each divides into lobar bronchi.
distractorExplanations.D: Approximately ten describes bronchopulmonary segments, not lobar bronchi.

learningObjective: Relate the number of lobar bronchi to pulmonary lobes.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchial tree — lobar bronchi

subject: anatomy
prompt: A surgeon plans to remove one bronchopulmonary segment while preserving neighboring segments. Which paired structures supply the functional unit being removed?

options.text: A lobar bronchus and the entire main pulmonary artery
A pulmonary vein and a main bronchus
An intercostal artery and a pleural recess
A segmental bronchus and its accompanying pulmonary artery branch

explanation: A bronchopulmonary segment is supplied by a tertiary bronchus with an accompanying branch of the pulmonary artery.

distractorExplanations.A: These supply territories larger than a single bronchopulmonary segment.
distractorExplanations.B: A main bronchus supplies a whole lung, while pulmonary veins tend to run between segments.
distractorExplanations.C: These are not the defining airway and arterial supply of a lung segment.

learningObjective: Define a bronchopulmonary segment by its airway and arterial supply.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchopulmonary segments — segmental supply

subject: anatomy
prompt: During anatomical segmentectomy, which vessels are typically encountered between neighboring bronchopulmonary segments rather than centrally accompanying a segmental bronchus?
explanation: Pulmonary venous tributaries tend to run between and around segment margins, whereas segmental bronchi and pulmonary arteries supply the segments.

distractorExplanations.B: These accompany the segmental bronchi into the bronchopulmonary segments.
distractorExplanations.C: The pulmonary trunk is in the mediastinum and divides before the arteries enter the lungs.
distractorExplanations.D: These run along the anterior thoracic wall and do not define intersegmental pulmonary planes.

learningObjective: Distinguish intersegmental pulmonary veins from intrasegmental bronchovascular structures.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Bronchopulmonary segments — intersegmental veins

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which two lobes are separated by the horizontal fissure of the right lung?

options.text: Superior and inferior lobes of the left lung

explanation: The right horizontal fissure separates the superior lobe from the middle lobe; the oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from both.

distractorExplanations.A: The oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from the superior and middle lobes.
distractorExplanations.B: These are separated by part of the oblique fissure, not the horizontal fissure.
distractorExplanations.C: The left lung has an oblique fissure but no normal horizontal fissure.

learningObjective: Identify the lobes adjacent to the right horizontal fissure.

subject: anatomy
prompt: A tongue-like projection extends from the anterior border of the left lung over the cardiac bulge. To which lobe does it belong?

options.text: Inferior lobe of the left lung
Middle lobe of the left lung
Superior lobe of the left lung
Middle lobe of the right lung

explanation: The lingula projects from the lower part of the left superior lobe; it is not a separate middle lobe.

distractorExplanations.A: The lingula is anterior and belongs to the superior, not the inferior, lobe.
distractorExplanations.B: The normal left lung has no separate middle lobe.
distractorExplanations.D: The described projection is the left lingula, not the right middle lobe.

learningObjective: Identify the lingula as part of the left superior lobe.

source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Left lung — lingula

subject: anatomy
prompt: A nerve is seen descending immediately anterior to the root of a lung. Which nerve is most consistent with this relationship?
explanation: The phrenic nerve passes immediately anterior to the lung root; the vagus passes immediately posterior.

distractorExplanations.A: The vagus runs posterior, not anterior, to the lung root.
distractorExplanations.B: Intercostal nerves follow intercostal spaces rather than descending across the front of the lung root.
distractorExplanations.D: XII is a cranial nerve of the tongue and does not descend past the lung root.

learningObjective: Distinguish phrenic and vagus nerve relationships to the lung root.

source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Root and hilum — neighboring nerves

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Root and hilum — right superior lobar bronchus
prompt: Which structure normally lies superior to the pulmonary artery within the root of the right lung?
explanation: On the right, the superior lobar bronchus branches within the root and lies above the pulmonary artery.

distractorExplanations.B: Pulmonary veins occupy the inferior part of the root rather than lying above this artery.
distractorExplanations.C: The pulmonary ligament extends inferiorly from the root.
distractorExplanations.D: The left main bronchus is a structure of the left lung root, not the right.

learningObjective: Recognize the eparterial position of the right superior lobar bronchus.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Root and hilum — right superior lobar bronchus

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Bronchial arteries and veins — nutritive circulation
prompt: Which arterial system supplies the bronchial walls and glands, walls of large pulmonary vessels, and visceral pleura as their nutritive circulation?
explanation: Bronchial arteries provide the nutritive vascular supply of these pulmonary tissues and connect with pulmonary vessels within the lung.

distractorExplanations.A: Pulmonary arteries deliver deoxygenated blood for gas exchange; the named nutritive system is the bronchial circulation.
distractorExplanations.C: Coronary arteries supply the heart, not the bronchial walls and visceral pleura.
distractorExplanations.D: These descend into the anterior abdominal wall and are not the pulmonary nutritive vessels.

learningObjective: Distinguish bronchial nutritive supply from pulmonary gas-exchange circulation.

subject: anatomy
prompt: In an upright patient, pleural fluid accumulates in the large recess between the inferior lung margin and the inferior pleural reflection. Which recess is this?
explanation: This recess lies between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, below the inferior lung edge, and is a potential site of fluid collection.

distractorExplanations.B: This lies anteriorly where costal and mediastinal pleura oppose one another, not along the inferior lung margin.
distractorExplanations.C: The hilum is the entry and exit area for root structures, not this inferior pleural recess.
distractorExplanations.D: The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart and is separate from the pleural cavity.

learningObjective: Identify the costodiaphragmatic recess as a site of pleural fluid accumulation.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Pleural recesses — costodiaphragmatic recess

subject: anatomy
subtopic: Pleural reflections and inferior lung border
prompt: During quiet respiration, which rib levels approximately mark the inferior lung border and the inferior pleural reflection at the midaxillary line?

options.text: Lung at rib 6; pleura at rib 8
Lung at rib 10; pleura at rib 12
Lung at rib 8; pleura at rib 10

explanation: At the midaxillary line the lung reaches approximately rib 8 while the pleural cavity extends to rib 10, leaving a recess below the lung.

distractorExplanations.A: These are the usual midclavicular, not midaxillary, landmarks.
distractorExplanations.B: These values do not describe the midaxillary rib landmarks; posterior limits are described using vertebral levels.
distractorExplanations.D: The pleural reflection extends farther inferiorly than the lung edge and therefore leaves a recess.

learningObjective: Compare lung and pleural lower borders at the midaxillary line.

source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Pleural reflections and inferior lung border

subject: anatomy
prompt: Irritation of the mediastinal pleura is felt near the shoulder rather than being sharply localized over the lateral chest wall. Which nerve carries the relevant pleural afferents?
explanation: Mediastinal pleural afferents travel mainly with the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), accounting for referral toward the neck and supraclavicular shoulder region.

distractorExplanations.B: They supply costal pleura, whose pain is felt in relation to the thoracic wall.
distractorExplanations.C: The vagus contributes to pulmonary visceral innervation, not the somatic afferent supply specified here.
distractorExplanations.D: This nerve supplies serratus anterior and is not the sensory nerve of the mediastinal pleura.

learningObjective: Relate mediastinal pleural sensation to phrenic referred pain.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Parietal pleura — phrenic sensory supply

subject: anatomy
prompt: Which nerves account for localized thoracic-wall pain caused by irritation of the costal pleura?
explanation: The costal parietal pleura receives somatic afferents through intercostal nerves, allowing pain to be felt in the corresponding thoracic wall.

distractorExplanations.A: Phrenic nerves mainly supply mediastinal and diaphragmatic pleural sensation, not the costal territory asked about.
distractorExplanations.B: Vagal pulmonary branches are not the somatic sensory supply of costal pleura.
distractorExplanations.C: These supply laryngeal structures and do not supply the costal pleura.

learningObjective: Identify somatic sensory innervation of the costal pleura.

source.title: Gray's Anatomy for Students
source.chapter: 3 — Thorax; Parietal pleura — costal sensory supply

subject: anatomy
prompt: Air entering the pleural cavity allows a lung to recoil and collapse. Between which two surfaces has the air accumulated?

options.text: Visceral pleura and the lung surface to which it adheres

explanation: The pleural cavity is the potential space between visceral pleura covering the lung and parietal pleura lining the thoracic boundaries.

distractorExplanations.B: Visceral pleura is firmly attached to the lung; the normal pleural cavity is external to it.
distractorExplanations.C: That is the pericardial cavity, not the pleural space.
distractorExplanations.D: This is within the airway wall and is not the cavity surrounding the lung.

learningObjective: Identify the pleural potential space involved in pneumothorax.

subject: anatomy
prompt: A thin fold of pleura extends inferiorly from the lung root toward the mediastinum. Which structure is being identified?
explanation: The pulmonary ligament is the blade-like pleural fold extending inferiorly from the lung root and hilum toward the mediastinum.

distractorExplanations.A: This is a vascular remnant connecting the pulmonary arterial region and aortic arch, not a fold descending from the hilum.
distractorExplanations.C: The suprapleural membrane is fascia over the cervical pleura at the thoracic inlet.
distractorExplanations.D: An oblique fissure separates pulmonary lobes; it is not the pleural fold below the root.

learningObjective: Recognize the pulmonary ligament as an inferior pleural fold.
